Chapter 1 · Topic 1

Electron displacement effects

GOC (General Organic Chemistry)General Organic ChemistryTopic 1 of 34

Explanation

Concept. Electron displacement effects (GOC (General Organic Chemistry), topic 1/34) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
Compare resonance $>$ hyperconjugation $>$ $+I$; $-I$ falls with distance
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Electron displacement effects” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 1 · Topic 6

Hyperconjugation

GOC (General Organic Chemistry)General Organic ChemistryTopic 6 of 34

Explanation

Concept. Hyperconjugation (GOC (General Organic Chemistry), topic 6/34) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$\\sigma(C{-}H)\\rightarrow p(C^+)$; $(CH_3)_3C^+>(CH_3)_2CH^+>CH_3CH_2^+>CH_3^+$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Hyperconjugation” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.

Concept. Benzyne mechanism (Halogen Derivatives, topic 23/29) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
Wurtz $2RX+2Na\\to R{-}R$; Finkelstein $RX+I^-\\to RI$; check selectivity first
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Benzyne mechanism” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Concept. Preparation using Grignard reagents (Alcohols and Ethers, topic 15/26) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$RX+Mg\\to RMgX$ (dry ether); $HCHO\\to1^\\circ$, $RCHO\\to2^\\circ$, $RCOR\\to3^\\circ$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Preparation using Grignard reagents” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Oxidation of carbonyls

Carbonyl CompoundsOxygen Functional GroupsTopic 10 of 32

Explanation

Concept. Oxidation of carbonyls (Carbonyl Compounds, topic 10/32) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$RCH_2OH\\xrightarrow{PCC}RCHO\\xrightarrow{Cr(VI)}RCOOH$; $3^\\circ$ alcohol resists
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Oxidation of carbonyls” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Q. Two substrates on “Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

$C_6H_6+E^+\\to[C_6H_6E]^+\\to C_6H_5E$; $o,p$: $OH,NH_2,R,X$; $m$: $NO_2,CN,COR$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Reimer-Tiemann reaction” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 8 · Topic 17

Mutarotation

BiomoleculesBiomolecules & Applied ChemistryTopic 17 of 30

Explanation

Concept. Mutarotation (Biomolecules, topic 17/30) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}+H_2O\\to2C_6H_{12}O_6$; A=T (2 bonds), G=C (3 bonds)
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Mutarotation” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Concept. Drug-target interaction (Chemistry in Everyday Life, topic 2/12) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
Soap $RCOONa$ micelle, scum in hard water; detergent $RSO_3Na$ works
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Drug-target interaction” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 12 · Topic 1

Classification of hydrocarbons

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons & Halo CompoundsTopic 1 of 41

Explanation

Concept. Classification of hydrocarbons (Hydrocarbons, topic 1/41) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$sp^3$ $109.5^\\circ$, $sp^2$ $120^\\circ$, $sp$ $180^\\circ$; $DBE=C-H/2+N/2+1$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Classification of hydrocarbons” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Alkynes: preparation and properties

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons & Halo CompoundsTopic 11 of 41

Explanation

Concept. Alkynes: preparation and properties (Hydrocarbons, topic 11/41) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$C_nH_{2n+2}$/$C_nH_{2n}$/$C_nH_{2n-2}$; acetylene $pK_a\\approx25$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Alkynes: preparation and properties” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 14 · Topic 1

Introduction to organometallics

Organometallic CompoundsSynthesis & ReactionsTopic 1 of 19

Explanation

Concept. Introduction to organometallics (Organometallic Compounds, topic 1/19) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$RX+Mg\\to RMgX$ (dry ether); $HCHO\\to1^\\circ$, $RCHO\\to2^\\circ$, $RCOR\\to3^\\circ$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Introduction to organometallics” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Reduction in organic chemistry

ReductionSynthesis & ReactionsTopic 1 of 25

Explanation

Concept. Reduction in organic chemistry (Reduction, topic 1/25) is a high-weight JEE idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$NaBH_4$: aldehyde/ketone only; $LiAlH_4$: acids/esters/amides/nitriles; Lindlar to cis
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Reduction in organic chemistry” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

$IHD=(2C+2+N-H-X)/2$; $C_4H_{10}O$=7 (4 alcohols+3 ethers)
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most JEE MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Counting structural isomers” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Oxidation reactions” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (JEE test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.
